title: How ELMA-IoT works
summary: Understand the builder, project, firmware runtime, and online Help.
body: ELMA-IoT turns a board, selected hardware profiles, GPIO assignments, and a visual Logics graph into firmware for an ESP device.

The four parts

  1. Android or Windows builder: creates the project, validates pins and Logics, compiles firmware, and flashes by USB or OTA.
  2. Project configuration: stores the board, peripheral slots, GPIO bindings, network settings, and editable graph.
  3. ESP firmware: runs supported drivers and the bounded Logics runtime, then exposes a local web interface, MQTT, status, logs, and OTA.
  4. Online documentation: owns long-form Help. Applications carry stable topic IDs and remain usable when Help is offline.

Profile versus driver

A hardware profile can reserve pins and draw wiring without having a firmware runtime adapter. Every peripheral article reports both levels. Compilation rejects unsupported Logics capabilities rather than silently pretending they work.

Normal workflow

Choose board → add peripherals → review GPIO → inspect wiring → create Logics → validate → compile → flash → verify live state
Start with [[getting-started.first-15-minutes|Your first 15 minutes]], then learn [[building-devices|how peripherals form one device]].

title: Install and prepare ELMA-IoT
summary: Prepare Android or Windows, the ESP board, USB, network, and optional MQTT broker.
body:
Choose an application

Use Android for a phone/tablet workflow with local compilation, USB/OTA flashing, and the portrait Logics constructor. Use Windows for a larger canvas and the standalone offline compiler. Keep application and generated firmware versions together when reporting a problem.

Checklist

  • A supported ESP board whose exact module and flash/PSRAM variant you can identify.
  • A data-capable USB cable and stable power.
  • Only low-voltage test hardware for the first build.
  • Wi-Fi credentials and local reachability for OTA.
  • An MQTT broker only if the project uses MQTT.

First connection

  1. Select the exact board.
  2. Leave GPIO safety checks enabled.
  3. Enter Wi-Fi Station credentials and keep AP fallback enabled until reachability is proven.
  4. Save before compiling.
  5. For the first installation, use USB and wait for image verification plus configuration acknowledgement.
Do not connect mains, motors, pumps, valves, heaters, or bare relay contacts for the first test. Prove the controller with low-voltage hardware first.

title: Your first 15 minutes
summary: Create, flash, and verify a small working ELMA-IoT device.
body:
Outcome

You will create a saved project, flash it by USB, reach its web interface, and observe one safe input or status value.

1. Create the project

  1. Use a descriptive filename such as desk-test.config.json.
  2. Select the exact ESP board; this controls reserved pins, ADC capability, flash target, and assignments.
  3. Add one low-voltage peripheral only after reading its page.
  4. Keep automatic GPIO selection unless the physical board forces a change.
  5. Compare the Graphic Designer wiring with the printed module labels.

2. Identity and network

  1. Set a unique name such as desk-test.
  2. Enter Wi-Fi credentials and keep AP fallback enabled.
  3. If using MQTT, enter broker, credentials, unique client ID, and base topic; otherwise leave host empty.

3. Compile and flash

  1. Save and resolve every blocking validation message.
  2. Compile for the selected board.
  3. Connect a data USB cable and choose the correct serial device.
  4. Wait for write verification, reset, Wi-Fi connection, and configuration acknowledgement.

4. Verify

  1. Open the reported IP address.
  2. Check board identity, firmware version, Wi-Fi signal, memory, and configured peripherals.
  3. Open Serial Monitor and reset once if anything is missing.
  4. Save a known-good project backup.

Success

The device boots repeatedly, reconnects, reports the expected hardware, and shows no pin-conflict or initialization error.
